name: Never Too Much
description: Never Too Much is the debut solo album by Luther Vandross, released in 1981 on Epic Records. After a decade as an elite background vocalist and a stint fronting the group Change, Vandross arrived with complete command of his instrument and his arrangements. The title track, bright and bouncing, became his signature song; “Don’t You Know That?” and his reading of “A House Is Not a Home” displayed the ballad control that would define the R&B love song for a decade. The album opened an unbroken run of eleven consecutive platinum albums, a streak the standard biographies record as a first for an R&B artist of his era, and it established the template — immaculate production, conversational phrasing, choruses built to be lived in — that Vandross refined for the rest of his career. Never Too Much is the sound of a singer who had spent ten years learning exactly where the microphone was, stepping up to it at last on his own name.

name: Nikki Giovanni
description: Nikki Giovanni (born Yolanda Cornelia Giovanni, June 7, 1943, Knoxville, Tennessee; died December 9, 2024, Virginia) was a poet, writer, and educator who emerged as a leading voice of the Black Arts Movement. Educated at Fisk University, where she graduated in 1967, she published her first volumes, Black Feeling, Black Talk (1968) and Black Judgment (1969), followed by Re: Creation (1970), and went on to write dozens of poetry collections, essays, and eleven illustrated children's books. Her honors included seven NAACP Image Awards for Literature, the Langston Hughes Award, and the Frost Medal for lifetime achievement in poetry. Giovanni taught at Rutgers from 1969 and at Virginia Tech from 1987 to 2022, where she was named University Distinguished Professor and remained on the faculty until her death. Her work moved between public witness — race, history, and collective grief — and an intimate register of family, place, and joy.

name: National Negro Labor Council
description: The National Negro Labor Council was an early-1950s Black labor and civil-rights organization — described in the reporting on its files as 'one of the most important civil rights organizations of the early 1950s' — driven out of existence by anti-communist pressure. Its documentary afterlife is a preservation loss: flooding during Hurricane Sandy in 2012 destroyed, at the FBI's archives in Alexandria, Virginia, 41 volumes (likely more than 8,000 pages) of the FBI's headquarters main file on the Council. The loss surfaced through a Freedom of Information Act response and was reported in 2014. Those were the FBI's surveillance files about the organization, not the Council's own papers — an adjacent, but distinct, erasure.

name: Neighborhood Tavern
description: Neighborhood Tavern is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice, Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000049, 'Neighborhood Taverns' (2026-10-09). The brief describes the tavern as the room with no agenda: musicians tried out songs, writers held court, and the neighborhood handled its business over drinks. Its documented examples are named rooms. Gerri's Palm Tavern was a historic Bronzeville tavern on 47th Street and a gathering place for jazz musicians and writers. Theresa's Lounge, a South Side blues room run by Theresa Needham, was a haunt of Chess bluesmen, tying the tavern to the recording industry's musicians. The C and C Lounge at 6513 S. Cottage Grove anchored a Woodlawn jazz nightlife district. The brief's general claim — taverns as informal cultural infrastructure — is graded PROVISIONAL; the three named-room claims are graded SUPPORTED.

name: Nina Simone
description: Nina Simone (born Eunice Kathleen Waymon on February 21, 1933, in Tryon, North Carolina; died April 21, 2003, in Carry-le-Rouet, France) was an American singer, pianist, and civil-rights activist. Classically trained, she studied briefly at Juilliard and was denied admission to the Curtis Institute — a rejection she believed was racial — then began singing in an Atlantic City nightclub in 1954 under a stage name. Her 1958 hit “I Loves You, Porgy” launched a career of more than forty albums blending jazz, blues, gospel, folk, and classical music. After the 1963 Birmingham church bombing she wrote “Mississippi Goddam”; “Four Women” and “Young, Gifted and Black” made her one of the movement's defining voices. She is remembered by the honorific “High Priestess of Soul.” She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018.

name: Negro National League
aliases: NNL; National Association of Colored Professional Base Ball Clubs
description: The Negro National League (NNL) was the first successful professional baseball league for African American players. It was founded on February 13, 1920, when Rube Foster and fellow team owners met at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri, and organized a governing body, the National Association of Colored Professional Base Ball Clubs. Its eight charter clubs — the Chicago American Giants, Chicago Giants, Cuban Stars, Dayton Marcos, Detroit Stars, Indianapolis ABCs, Kansas City Monarchs, and St. Louis Giants — gave Black baseball a stable schedule, honored player contracts, and a pennant race for the first time. Foster, the league's president, ran it from Chicago, where his American Giants were its flagship team. The league expanded into the South in 1924 and met the Eastern Colored League in the first Colored World Series that year. Weakened after Foster's institutionalization in 1926 and his death in 1930, the league collapsed in 1931.

name: National Park Service
description: The National Park Service (NPS) is the United States federal agency, within the Department of the Interior, charged with caring for the National Park System. Congress created it on August 25, 1916, through the National Park Service Organic Act, unifying parks and monuments that had been managed piecemeal; its first director was Stephen T. Mather. The Organic Act's mandate — to conserve scenery, natural and historic objects, and wildlife, and to leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations — still governs a system of more than 430 units covering over 85 million acres in every state, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. In CultureTechLens research, the Service is the administering authority of the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument, established by presidential proclamation on July 25, 2023, whose three sites include Chicago's Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ, where Emmett Till's open-casket funeral was held in 1955.

name: NBA YoungBoy
aliases: Kentrell DeSean Gaulden; YoungBoy Never Broke Again; YB
description: NBA YoungBoy, born Kentrell DeSean Gaulden on October 20, 1999, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, is a rapper whose prolific output and direct-to-fan streaming audience made him one of the most-charted artists of his generation. Recording from his mid-teens and releasing through his Never Broke Again imprint, he signed with Atlantic Records in 2017; his mixtape AI YoungBoy was his first Billboard 200 entry that year, and his debut studio album, Until Death Call My Name (2018), reached the top 10. Between 2019 and 2021 he placed four projects at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — AI YoungBoy 2, 38 Baby 2, Top, and Sincerely, Kentrell, the last released while he was jailed awaiting trial. His highest-charting single, "Bandit" with Juice WRLD, reached No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 2019, and in May 2023, at 23, he became the youngest artist in Billboard history to chart 100 songs on the Hot 100. His career has run alongside repeated arrests and periods of incarceration and house arrest, which the music addresses directly.

name: National Syndication Launch of The Oprah Winfrey Show (1986)
aliases: Oprah Winfrey Launches Syndicated Talk Show; The Oprah Winfrey Show Goes National
description: On September 8, 1986, The Oprah Winfrey Show was broadcast nationally for the first time, syndicated by King World — the event the intake timeline files as 'Oprah Winfrey Launches Syndicated Talk Show.' The show had begun in Chicago, where Winfrey arrived in 1984 to host WLS-TV's AM Chicago and turned the market's lowest-rated morning program into its leader, overtaking Phil Donahue's local ratings within months. On the advice of Chicago film critic Roger Ebert, who predicted the syndicated show would out-earn his own many times over, Winfrey signed the King World deal, and the renamed, hour-long program launched in markets across the country at once. It became the highest-rated daytime talk show in American television history, ran for twenty-five seasons, and built the platform from which Winfrey — held at CTL-E-0092, with her Harpo (CTL-E-1627) and OWN (CTL-E-0712) elsewhere in the graph — became the defining media proprietor of her generation. The stop matters to this graph doubly: it is a national milestone whose studio address was always Chicago.

name: Negro American League
description: The Negro American League (NAL) was a professional Black baseball league organized in February 1937, uniting the strongest clubs of the Midwest and South in the era when organized baseball barred Black players. Its eight charter clubs included Chicago's Chicago American Giants and the Kansas City Monarchs, who won five of the league's first six pennants and eight league titles in all. From 1942, the league's champion met the Negro National League champion in a revived Negro World Series. The NAL was Chicago's big-league Black baseball home: the American Giants, charter members under owner Dr. J. B. Martin, anchored the league's western circuit. When the Negro National League folded after 1948, the NAL absorbed four of its clubs and continued at minor-league level until its final season in 1962, diminished as integration drained its rosters. In December 2020, Major League Baseball recognized the Negro leagues — the NAL among them — as major leagues for the 1920–1948 period.

name: New Life Covenant Church Southeast
aliases: New Life Covenant Southeast; NLCSE; NLC Southeast
description: New Life Covenant Church Southeast is a nondenominational, multicultural congregation on Chicago's South Side founded and led by Pastor John F. Hannah. Church accounts describe a start on January 27, 2010, with about sixty people at a Wednesday-night Bible study. The congregation became known for an intense prayer culture — 4 AM prayer gatherings, twelve-hour prayer events, and the annual Prayer on the 9 march that lines 79th Street — and worshiped at a site it calls The Tabernacle, at 78th and Dobson. In September 2021 it opened The Temple, a 100,000-square-foot, 4,000-seat worship and performing-arts facility at 7621 South Greenwood Avenue in Greater Grand Crossing, a project Hannah framed as economic redevelopment of an underserved African American community. The record is distinct from the separate, older New Life Covenant Church in Humboldt Park.

name: Nia Archives
description: Nia Archives (born Dehaney Nia Lishahn Hunt, September 1999, in Bradford, West Yorkshire, England) is an English producer, DJ, and singer-songwriter at the forefront of the post-2020 jungle and drum-and-bass revival. Raised in Leeds from age seven and later based in Manchester and London, she broke through with the self-released EPs Headz Gone West (2021), Forbidden Feelingz (2022), and Sunrise Bang Ur Head Against the Wall (2023), the last of which topped the UK Dance Albums Chart. In 2022 her open letter prompted the MOBO Awards to add a Best Electronic/Dance Act category — which she then won. Her debut album Silence Is Loud (2024, Island Records) peaked at No. 16 on the UK Albums Chart; her second album, Emotional Junglist — the subject of CTL Short #46 — followed in 2026.

name: Nubiyan Twist
description: Nubiyan Twist is a nine-piece British group formed in 2011 at Leeds College of Music around guitarist and producer Tom Excell, blending jazz, Afrobeat, soul, and electronic music into a horn-driven live sound. The group released its self-titled debut album on Wormfood Records in 2015, followed by Jungle Run (2019) and Freedom Fables (2021) on Strut Records, Find Your Flame (2024), and Chasing Shadows (2026), whose title track features Malian singer Fatoumata Diawara. Across that run the band has worked with vocalists and players drawn from across the African diaspora and the United Kingdom's jazz scene, building a reputation as one of the defining live acts of the new UK jazz generation. name: Nightcap
aliases: The Nightcap with Unc and Ocho
description: Nightcap is a nightly sports-talk podcast and video show hosted by Shannon Sharpe and Chad 'Ochocinco' Johnson, premiering in September 2023 on the Club Shay Shay YouTube channel as 'The Nightcap with Unc and Ocho' before spinning out to its own channel in October 2023. Produced by The Volume and Shay Shay Media, it mixes same-night game reaction with the hosts' unscripted banter, and it debuted at number 46 on the Top 50 U.S. Podcasts chart. Former NBA player Gilbert Arenas co-hosted from December 2023 to June 2024, and former NBA guard Joe Johnson became an official co-host in April 2025; a live HBCU tour followed the show's growth. CultureTechLens's Short covers the program; neither the show nor its hosts held CultureTechLens records before this packet — the reverse gap closed here, with Sharpe and Johnson named as further person gaps.

name: Negril Universal Film Festival
description: The Negril Universal Film Festival (NUFF) is a beachfront film festival held on Seven Mile Beach in Negril, Jamaica, hosted at the Skylark Negril Beach Resort and organized by the Jamaica Film and Television Association (JAFTA) with international partners. The 2026 edition, held October 8–11, was the festival's seventh year and its first under the NUFF name, succeeding the Skylark Film Festival. It screened thirty-four films from thirteen countries, drawn from more than 2,700 submissions, with open-air evening screenings and daytime master classes on film finance, distribution and vertical filmmaking. The program opened with a twenty-fifth-anniversary screening of Stephanie Black's Life and Debt, included a tribute to Jimmy Cliff and the Jamaican premiere of Reggae Girlz, and closed with the maternal-health documentary Listen to Me followed by a public policy discussion. CultureTechLens covered the festival in Short #141, published October 14, 2026.

name: N3ON
description: N3ON, born Rangesh Mutama on August 13, 2004, is an American live streamer and internet personality. He began making gaming content on YouTube in May 2016, at about age eleven, concentrating on NBA 2K and Fortnite, and later moved into live streaming on Twitch and then Kick, where he became one of the platform's most-watched IRL streamers; a 2026 industry profile credits him with roughly 765,000 Kick followers and 1.17 million YouTube subscribers. His rise was powered in part by a paid clipping network that distributes short clips of his streams across social platforms, a model reported to have cost about $1.4 million over five weeks. His career has also drawn documented controversy, reported neutrally here: a 2024 detention in Dubai over filming without permission, a 2024 Kick ban, and a September 2024 Twitch suspension. In August 2026 the crypto casino JACK.com announced signing him to lead its United States creator push, and Business Insider has described him as one of Kick's top stars.

description: NLE Choppa, born Bryson LaShun Potts on 1 November 2002 in Memphis, Tennessee, and raised in the Parkway Village neighborhood, is an American rapper. Freestyling from age fifteen, he broke through with "Shotta Flow" in January 2019, which reached No. 36 on the Billboard Hot 100 and was certified platinum by the RIAA. After an initial UnitedMasters partnership he formed a Warner Records joint venture for his No Love Entertainment label. His releases run from the EP Cottonwood (2019) through Top Shotta (2020), which reached No. 10 on the Billboard 200, to Cottonwood 2 (2023); he was a 2020 XXL Freshman. The "Slut Me Out" remix (2023) became his highest Hot 100 entry, in the top 30, and in 2025 he rebranded publicly as NLE the Great and opened on Lil Baby's WHAM World Tour.

name: N.W.A
description: N.W.A was an American hip-hop group from Compton, California, and the act Ice Cube's record in this graph has pointed to without holding. The original lineup, formed in early 1987, consisted of Arabian Prince, Dr. Dre, Eazy-E and Ice Cube, with DJ Yella and MC Ren joining later that year. Their debut studio album, Straight Outta Compton (1988), marked the beginning of the gangsta rap era, its production and social commentary drawn from the members' own experiences of racism and excessive policing, and it drew an FBI response and widespread radio bans while selling in the millions. Arabian Prince left shortly after the debut, and Ice Cube followed in December 1989. The remaining lineup's Niggaz4Life (1991) became the first hardcore rap album to reach number one on the Billboard 200, and the group disbanded shortly after its release. Eazy-E died on March 26, 1995. Straight Outta Compton entered the Library of Congress National Recording Registry in 2017, the group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2016 after three previous nominations, and it received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2024. Of its members, Ice Cube (CTL-E-5698) and Dr. Dre (CTL-E-5355) hold records in this graph.

name: Nick Cannon
description: Nick Cannon, born Nicholas Scott Cannon on 8 October 1980 in San Diego, California, is an American comedian, actor, rapper and television host who has been a fixture of youth television since his teens. Raised largely in Lincoln Park's Bay Vista housing projects in Southeast San Diego and a 1998 graduate of Monte Vista High School, he broke in through stand-up comedy and joined Nickelodeon's sketch series All That as a teenager, also writing for the show. Film leads followed in Drumline (2002) and Love Don't Cost a Thing (2003), alongside a recording career launched by his self-titled debut album in 2003. His defining creation is Wild 'n Out, the improvised comedy-battle series he created and hosts, launched on MTV in 2005 and still running two decades later. He hosted NBC's America's Got Talent for eight seasons and has hosted Fox's The Masked Singer since its 2019 debut, while running his NCredible Entertainment company. In 2020 he completed a bachelor's degree at Howard University in criminology and administration of justice, four years after enrolling at the HBCU.

name: Neymar
aliases: Neymar Jr.; Neymar da Silva Santos Júnior
description: Neymar, in full Neymar da Silva Santos Júnior, born 5 February 1992 in Mogi das Cruzes, Brazil, is a Brazilian footballer who plays as a forward or attacking midfielder. He debuted for Santos in 2009 and helped the club win the Copa Libertadores in 2011, then joined Barcelona in 2013, where the attacking trio he formed with Lionel Messi and Luis Suárez won the continental treble in 2014–15. In 2017 he moved to Paris Saint-Germain in a world-record transfer, won multiple Ligue 1 titles, and reached the 2020 Champions League final; after a spell with Al-Hilal he returned to Santos in January 2025. For Brazil, in official FIFA matches, he scored his 78th and 79th international goals against Bolivia in September 2023, passing Pelé's official tally of 77 to become the men's team's all-time top scorer.

name: National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses
aliases: NCGCC; National Convention of Gospel Choirs & Choruses
description: The National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses (NCGCC) is the founding national organization of organized gospel choral music in the United States. A first gospel choral union was organized in Chicago in 1932, with Thomas A. Dorsey elected its president, and on August 30, 1933, at Pilgrim Baptist Church in Chicago, the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses was organized and held its first session. Dorsey, known as the Father of Gospel Music, founded the convention after recognizing a need to organize gospel choirs collectively into unions, and BlackPast records that singer Sallie Martin co-founded it with him in 1933. The convention is recorded as the first of its kind. Dorsey remained its president for six decades. Its annual week-long session is built around classes, educational workshops, lecture sessions and nightly concerts, designed for the betterment of the Christian singer, instrumentalist, educator and leader, and the organization continues to hold annual sessions under later leadership, including President Dr. Marabeth E. Gentry in the sources consulted.

name: National Bankers Association
aliases: Negro Bankers Association; National Negro Bankers Association
description: The National Bankers Association is the trade association of America's minority-owned banks, founded in 1927 as the Negro Bankers Association. Its organizing meeting brought nineteen Black banks together at Pythias Hall in Philadelphia in 1926, led by R. R. Wright of Philadelphia and C. C. Spaulding of Durham, North Carolina; the founding meeting followed in Durham in 1927. Renamed the National Bankers Association in 1948, it is headquartered in Washington, D.C., and describes itself as the voice of minority banking. Its membership — about one hundred institutions in the association's recent counts — spans twenty-two states and the District of Columbia, and has expanded beyond Black-owned banks to Hispanic-American, Asian-American, Native American, and women-owned institutions. For nearly a century the association has been the organized form of Black America's banking sector, the industry that financed much of the world this graph records.

name: Natalie Y. Moore
description: Natalie Y. Moore is a Chicago-native journalist and author whose reporting on segregation and inequality made her one of Black Chicago's defining contemporary chroniclers. She joined Chicago's WBEZ in 2007 and became its South Side reporter, covering race, housing, economic development, food injustice, and violence, with work broadcast by the BBC, Marketplace, and NPR and published in outlets including the Chicago Sun-Times, where she wrote a monthly column, the Chicago Tribune, the New York Times, the Washington Post, and the Guardian. Before WBEZ she reported for the Detroit News, the St. Paul Pioneer Press, and the Associated Press in Jerusalem. Her book The South Side: A Portrait of Chicago and American Segregation won the 2016 Chicago Review of Books award for nonfiction, and she co-authored The Almighty Black P Stone Nation and Deconstructing Tyrone. She holds a journalism degree from Howard University and a master's from Northwestern's Medill School, received the Chicago Library Foundation's 21st Century Award in 2017, and was named the Chicago Reader's best journalist that year. In April 2026 she moderated a Chicago journalism panel as a Medill lecturer.

name: Nia Sioux
description: Nia Sioux Frazier, born 20 June 2001 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, is an American dancer, actress, singer and author. The daughter of Holly and Evan Frazier, she began training at the Abby Lee Dance Company at age three and was cast at nine, with her mother, on Lifetime's Dance Moms, appearing in all seven seasons from 2011 to 2017 as the team's longest-serving member and, for most of the run, its only Black dancer. Frequently ranked at the bottom of the show's weekly pyramid, she also released singles including "Star in Your Own Life" and "Slay." She made her off-Broadway debut in Trip of Love in 2016 and played Emma Barber on CBS's The Bold and the Beautiful from 2018 to 2019. She graduated from UCLA in 2024. Her memoir, Bottom of the Pyramid, was published in November 2025 and became a New York Times bestseller; in 2026 she performed off-Broadway in 11 to Midnight and in Mean Girls at Pittsburgh CLO.

name: Natalie Nunn
description: Natalie Tynika Nunn, born 26 December 1984 in Concord, California, is an American reality television personality and executive producer. A track athlete who competed at the 2002 Junior Olympics, she attended the University of Southern California on a soccer scholarship and played as a defender for the Trojans in 2004. She rose to fame on the fourth season of Oxygen's Bad Girls Club in 2009, at the time the highest-rated premiere in the network's history, and returned across franchise spin-offs including Love Games: Bad Girls Need Love Too and Bad Girls All-Star Battle. In 2018 she competed on the United Kingdom's Celebrity Big Brother. Since 2021 she has been executive producer and main cast member of Zeus Network's Baddies, building the format through regional seasons from Baddies ATL to Baddies Africa and Baddies USA, and creating its spin-off Bad Boys in 2022. She discussed the franchise's reach in a March 2026 Rolling Out interview.

name: Naomi Campbell
description: Naomi Elaine Campbell, born 22 May 1970 in London, England, is a British fashion model and actress. The daughter of Jamaican-born dancer Valerie Morris-Campbell, she studied at the Barbara Speake Stage School and the Italia Conti Academy, appeared in Bob Marley's 'Is This Love' music video, and was scouted at fifteen. She appeared on the cover of British Elle in 1986, became in December 1987 the first British Black model on the cover of British Vogue, and in August 1988 the first Black model on the cover of French Vogue. One of six models of her generation declared supermodels, she has appeared on more than 500 magazine covers, walking for houses including Versace, Chanel, Prada and Louis Vuitton. She founded the charity Fashion for Relief in 2005, received the CFDA Fashion Icon Award in 2018, and remains active, making a DJ debut at Milan Fashion Week in 2026.

name: National Council of Negro Women
aliases: NCNW; National Council of Negro Women, Inc.
description: The National Council of Negro Women (NCNW) is a nonprofit civil-rights organization founded by Mary McLeod Bethune on December 5, 1935, in New York City. Bethune created it to give African American women a collective national voice and to unite existing organizations; NCNW describes itself as an organization of organizations. Its stated mission is to lead, advocate for, and empower women of African descent, their families and communities, with later wording also framed as advancing opportunities and quality of life. Bethune served as its first president, retiring in 1949, according to the National Park Service. Dorothy Height, elected fourth national president in 1957, led NCNW for decades; sources differ on whether her presidency ended in 1997 or 1998, when she became chair and president emerita. NCNW's first Washington headquarters was the Council House at 1318 Vermont Avenue, used from 1943 to 1966. In 1995 members dedicated a new headquarters at 633 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C., an address NCNW still lists as its headquarters.

name: New York Mets
aliases: The Metropolitans; The Amazin' Mets; The Amazin's; The Miracle Mets
description: The New York Mets are a Major League Baseball team based in Queens, New York City, competing in the National League East Division. Founded in 1962 as a National League expansion team to replace New York's departed Dodgers and Giants, the Mets played at the Polo Grounds in 1962 and 1963, at Shea Stadium from 1964 to 2008, and at Citi Field since 2009. After an inaugural 40–120 season, the "Miracle Mets" won the 1969 World Series over Baltimore, and the club won its second championship in 1986 over Boston. Hall of Famer Willie Mays returned to New York in a May 1972 trade and finished his career with the Mets in the 1973 World Series. In December 2024 the Mets agreed with Juan Soto on a reported record fifteen-year, $765 million contract, and Soto played the 2025 season in Queens. The franchise remains active, with its history, ballparks and championships documented by Britannica and league reporting.

name: Nina Idemudia
description: Nina Idemudia, AICP, is Chief Executive Officer of the Center for Neighborhood Technology (CNT), the Chicago urban-innovation organization founded in 1978; she joined as CEO in September 2023 after serving as Chicago Recovery Plan Director in the Chicago Department of Planning and Development, Director of Planning at MUSE Community + Design, and a planner for the City of Los Angeles. Crain's Chicago Business named her to its own 40 Under 40 in 2024, and she was elected the first Black president of the Illinois chapter of the American Planning Association in 2021. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
